FDB17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs

29 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1612Migration: court challengeMigration
The appellant, a Pakistani protection visa applicant, appealed a Federal Circuit and Family Court judgment dismissing his judicial review application concerning an AAT decision that affirmed refusal of his visa. He argued the Tribunal fell into jurisdictional error by unreasonably declining to telephone four corroborating witnesses (his parents, brother and a friend) who had already provided a joint signed statement. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the Tribunal's approach had a rational and intelligible foundation.
Key holding

Where a decision-maker is convinced that an applicant's account is fabricated or fundamentally unreliable, it is not irrational or illogical to decline to hear oral corroborating evidence and to reject that corroboration, even absent any independent ground for doubting the corroborators.

It is not necessarily irrational, or illogical, for a finder of fact, who is convinced that a principal witness is fabricating a story, which is considered to be inherently implausible, to reject corroborative evidence, even though there is no separate or independent ground for its rejection, apart from the reasons given for disbelieving the principal witness.

Jamdar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

28 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1620Migration: court challengeMigration
The Federal Court granted an extension of time but dismissed an appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had affirmed refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good-character grounds. The applicant challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of earlier non-conviction offending and its finding that he deliberately withheld his 2023 conviction.
Key holding

Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) precludes reliance on the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt, but does not preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Sections 85ZR and 85ZS are directed to the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt and do not expressly preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority

28 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1615Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.
Key holding

Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

EEN25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

27 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1600Migration: court challengeMigration
This was an application for leave to appeal from a Federal Circuit and Family Court decision summarily dismissing a judicial review application. The Court held the Tribunal lacked jurisdiction because the protection visa review application was lodged out of time, and refused leave.
Key holding

The Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to review a delegate’s decision where the review application is lodged outside the statutory 28-day period.

The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to hear the application made to it for review of the decision of the delegate, because the application to the Tribunal was made out of time.

Key holding

Under s 19(2) of the ART Act, delay is a relevant but not automatically determinative factor in the multifactorial assessment of reasonableness, and a very long delay may set a high bar for an applicant.

The nature of the multifactorial inquiry is such that there will invariably be cases where the gravity of one factor (eg delay) will be so great and will set the bar for the applicant so high that, as a general proposition, it will be unlikely that the factual matrix will be one where it is "reasonable in all the circumstances" for the Tribunal to exercise its discretion under s 19(2).

Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

27 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1602Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationCharacter testMigration
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs

26 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1586Migration: court challengeMigration
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.
Key holding

A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

23 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1589Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.
Key holding

Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

Harvey v State of Queensland

23 Oct 2026Queensland Court of Appeal[2026] QCA 214Migration: court challengeMigration
The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Harvey’s appeal from a decision refusing to set aside his notice of discontinuance of a police assault damages claim filed more than seven years earlier. The Court found no error in the primary judge’s discretionary conclusion that the appellant had not shown good reason, or that the interests of justice required, setting aside the discontinuance, given unparticularised evidence and unexplained delay.
Key holding

Even if a court may set aside a notice of discontinuance where the interests of justice require it, unparticularised claims of duress or mental illness and lengthy unexplained delay will not satisfy that test.

Assuming in the appellant's favour that the court had power to set aside the discontinuance if it was shown to be in the interests of justice to do so, the material before the primary judge did not satisfy that test.

Kola v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

22 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1550Migration: court challengeMigration
The Federal Court dismissed Mr Kola’s challenge to an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of citizenship by conferral under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). Darlington-Thomas v Elgas Limited

21 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1566Migration: court challengeMigration
The Federal Court granted Ms Darlington-Thomas leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) to proceed against her labour hire employer, Zoom, for alleged disability discrimination. The AHRC had terminated her complaint against Zoom, but the Court held the claim was reasonably arguable and should be resolved with the overlapping claim against Elgas.
Key holding

On an application for leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act, the Court asks only whether the proposed discrimination claim is reasonably arguable and not fanciful, rather than determining the merits.

I am satisfied that the text, context and purpose of the leave requirement in s 46PO(3A) suggests that it is appropriate for the Court to consider in determining whether to grant leave whether the claims made by an applicant are reasonably arguable, and are - at the least - not fanciful. This is consistent with the language used in s 46P(1A).

Watson v Director of Public Prosecutions (NSW)

21 Oct 2026New South Wales Court of Appeal[2026] NSWCA 222Migration: court challengeAdministrative law
Before: Stern JA at [1]Free JA at [2]Price AJA at [98] Decision: (1) The amended summons
Mr Watson sought judicial review in the NSW Court of Appeal of Beckett DCJ’s refusal under s 5B of the Criminal Appeal Act 1912 (NSW) to submit questions of law to the Court of Criminal Appeal after his conviction appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal dismissed the amended summons, holding that no jurisdictional error was shown in her Honour’s treatment of the proposed questions. Costs were awarded to the DPP.
Key holding

On judicial review of a s 5B decision, an error by the District Court in characterising a proposed question as law, fact or mixed fact and law is ordinarily an error of law within jurisdiction and therefore not a jurisdictional error.

As a consequence, an error by a judge, when determining an application under s 5B, in characterising a proposed question as a question of law, a question of fact, or a question of mixed law and fact, is ordinarily apt to be characterised as an error of law within jurisdiction.

BNE24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

20 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1561Migration: court challengeMigration
This was an appeal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing review of a Tribunal decision refusing a protection visa. The unrepresented appellant argued the Tribunal’s adverse credibility findings were illogical or unreasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the primary judge correctly found no jurisdictional error.
Key holding

A Tribunal’s adverse credibility finding does not involve jurisdictional error merely because a reviewing court would have reached a different factual finding; the reasoning must be legally unreasonable.

Therefore, jurisdictional error in the reasoning by the Tribunal as to the credibility of the account given by an applicant is not established by seeking to persuade a court on review that the Tribunal's reasoning includes an error in the sense that the Court would not make the same finding.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson

20 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1548Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.
Key holding

Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

Key holding

On an appeal from an interlocutory parenting discretion under s 60CC, an appellate court will not intervene absent a recognised House v The King error, including where the orders are a cautious stopgap pending expert assessment.

A discretionary determination is presumed to be correct unless and until error is established. Thus, to succeed in an appeal from the exercise of such a discretion, an appellant must bring their appeal within one of the recognised categories of appellate intervention identified by the High Court in House v The King (1936) 55 CLR 499.

Barresi v Cross Yarra Partnerships

19 Oct 2026Supreme Court of Victoria[2026] VSC 666Migration: court challengeMigration
Before: Clements J
The plaintiff sought judicial review of a second Wrongs Act Medical Panel determination that his whole person impairment did not meet the threshold, after an earlier panel had found that it did. The Court followed Citywide Service Solutions Pty Ltd v Rosata in permitting the later panel to determine the same medical question, and rejected the challenge based on s 28LZG(4). The catchwords record “Appeal dismissed”.
Key holding

An asserted misunderstanding by a Medical Panel of s 28LZG(4) will not constitute jurisdictional error unless the misunderstanding was material to the determination, in the sense that the decision could realistically have been different.

Consequently, in my opinion, the plaintiff has not established that the asserted misunderstanding by the second Panel of s 28LZG(4) was material to the decision that the second Panel made and therefore jurisdictional error has not been established.

GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

16 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1535Migration: court challengeMigration
GWN25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Minister conceded jurisdictional error in light of Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v DVRL, and the parties jointly proposed certiorari and mandamus. The Federal Court set aside the Tribunal decision and remitted the matter for redetermination, with costs.
Key holding

When assessing community risk under the relevant ministerial direction, the Tribunal must consider the different levels of risk depending on the visa status the applicant would hold, where that issue is advanced and supported by evidence.

The effect of the full court's ruling in DVRL is that the Tribunal was obliged, when considering "... the risk to the Australian community ..." for the purposes of cl 8.1(2) of the applicable ministerial direction, to consider not merely the risk that the applicant might pose if his permanent visa were restored but also the risk that he might pose as the holder of an ongoing bridging visa.

Foong v Health Care Complaints Commission

16 Oct 2026New South Wales Court of Appeal[2026] NSWCA 217Migration: court challengeMigration
Before: Ward ACJ at [1]Adamson JA at [2]McHugh JA at [66] Decision: (1) Grant leave to a
Dr Andrew Foong sought leave to appeal from NCAT’s refusal to recuse Principal Member Ainslie-Wallace AM ADCJ in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Health Care Complaints Commission. The alleged apprehended bias arose because the Principal Member had sat on a Medical Tribunal in 2010 with Dr Emery Kertesz, who was the Commission’s sole expert witness in the current proceedings. Key holding

A prior tribunal association with an expert witness will not, without more, create a reasonable apprehension of bias where the only feared influence is a favourable view of that expert’s expertise, and the expert’s credibility and relevant expertise are not in issue.

Here, the only relevant possibility was that the Principal Member had, by reason of prior association, formed and retained an attitude that Dr Kertesz had the expertise to give evidence as a general practitioner in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Commission against another general practitioner. This attitude had no potential to have any effect in the present proceedings as Dr Kertesz's expertise as a general practitioner was accepted.

Lye v Comcare

15 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1517Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationMigration
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.
Key holding

Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). The Tribunal decision was quashed and the matter remitted for determination according to law.
Key holding

Under Direction 110 [8.1.2(2)(c)], the Tribunal must consider whether and how the duration and purpose of an intended stay affect risk of harm to the Australian community, not whether the applicant satisfies substantive visa eligibility criteria.

The Tribunal erred by misapprehending the nature of the inquiry. It was required to consider, under [8.1.2(2)(c)] of Direction 110, how the duration and purpose of the intended stay affected the risk of harm to the Australian community, and misconstrued its task by considering the issue through the wrong lens (possible visa ineligibility).

It is not sufficient that the accessory merely knows that his or her conduct will assist the principal perpetrator in the commission of the offence.

Burgess & Burgess (No 2)

23 Sep 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1 First Instance)[2026] FedCFamC1F 649Migration: court challengeMigration
This was a part-heard family law property proceeding under s 79 of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) in which the wife sought to rely on a covert audio recording of the husband. After the High Court’s decision in Potter (A Pseudonym) v The King [2026] HCA 25, Parker J revisited an earlier interlocutory ruling admitting the recording, excluded it, recused herself, and aborted the trial. The husband was granted a costs certificate.
Key holding

In South Australia, s 9(1) of the Surveillance Devices Act 2016 (SA) (and by parity s 12(1)) is a law relating to evidence picked up by s 79(1) of the Judiciary Act and applies in federal family law proceedings, so a recording obtained for a lawful-interest purpose cannot be used unless a s 9(1) exception applies, and s 138 of the Evidence Act does not displace that prohibition.

In my view, subsection 9(1) is therefore a "law relating to evidence," the effect of which is that it is "picked up" by section 79 of the Judiciary Act[17] such that the same limitation applies in the context of a court exercising federal jurisdiction in South Australia, as is the case in the present proceeding. The same reasoning applies with respect to subsection 12(1) of the Surveillance Devices Act.

Key holding

For Commonwealth offences, the common law requirement that hardship to family be "exceptional" before it significantly mitigates sentence does not apply, because s 16A(2)(p) of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) directs the court to take into account the probable effect of the sentence on family or dependants according to its terms.

However, it has been clear in this state since the decision in Totaan [2022] NSWCCA 75, that this is not so in cases involving Commonwealth offences. That is because paragraph (p) of s 16A(2) makes specific reference to the need for the Court to take into account the probable effect on family or dependants.

This costs judgment follows the Minister’s successful appeal in Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v XMBQ [2026] FCAFC 19, in which the Full Court held that s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) is not subject to an implied reasonable-time limit. Reeve v Chartered Accountants of Australia and New Zealand (No 3) [2026] FCA 518 (29 April 2026)

29 Apr 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 518Migration: court challenge
Mr Reeve, a self-represented applicant, sought the recusal of Meagher J from his Fair Work Division proceeding against the Chartered Accountants of Australia and New Zealand and Mr Rice, alleging actual bias, apprehended bias, procedural unfairness, undisclosed conflicts and collusion. The applicant did not appear at the hearing; the Court refused any implied adjournment and dismissed the recusal application, listing remaining interlocutory matters for later hearing. Key holding

A judge is not required to recuse merely because a party asks; recusal is required only if actual or apprehended bias is established, otherwise the judge has a duty to sit.

Therefore, in deciding whether the evidence adduced by the Applicant satisfies the tests for either actual or apprehended bias, I must bear in mind that unless either of these tests is satisfied, I have a duty to sit and hear this matter.

EFS18 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 461 (17 April 2026)

17 Apr 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 461Migration: court challengeMigration
EFS18, an Egyptian national, sought judicial review of an Immigration Assessment Authority decision affirming refusal of a protection visa, which the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissed. He appealed to the Federal Court, raising grounds about unwarranted assumptions, country information, health issues, procedural fairness and legal unreasonableness. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal with costs.
Key holding

An alleged unwarranted assumption is not a separate ground of review but a rationality challenge, requiring proof that the assumption had no evident or intelligible basis and no reasonable decision-maker could make it.

This is not an independent ground of review but rather a particular instance of rationality review. A party seeking to rely upon an unwarranted assumption to establish jurisdictional error will need to show that the assumption is not one which a reasonable decision maker could make or, perhaps to paraphrase, that it does not have an evident or intelligible basis.

Chinacalle v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, Migrant Services and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 441 (16 April 2026)

16 Apr 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 441Migration: court challenge
Maria Chinacalle held a subclass 485 visa as a secondary visa holder based on her de facto relationship with the primary visa holder, Mr Ortega. After they separated, Mr Ortega’s visa was cancelled under s 116(1)(g), and her visa was cancelled under s 140(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). She sought a declaration that her visa was not cancelled because she was no longer a member of his family unit at the time of cancellation; the Federal Court dismissed her application.
Key holding

Section 140(1) automatically cancels a secondary visa that was held because of family-unit membership at the time of grant, regardless of whether that membership still existed when the primary visa was cancelled.

The proper construction of s 140(1) is that it cancels a secondary visa which was held by that other person because of being a member of the family unit of the first person, at the time the secondary person's visa was granted. If that first person's visa is cancelled (on certain bases) then that secondary person's visa is also cancelled.

Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs v SSVJ [2026] FCAFC 45 (13 April 2026)

13 Apr 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 45Migration: court challenge
Full Court appeal concerning cancellation under s 501BA of the Migration Act after the AAT had revoked the respondent’s visa cancellation. The Minister cancelled again relying on national interest and community protection despite accepting NZYQ meant no detention or removal. The Full Court dismissed the Minister’s appeal, holding the main appeal ground succeeded but the notice of contention established irrational current rehabilitation findings based on stale material.
Key holding

If the Minister exercises s 501BA(2) without hearing the visa holder and relies on materially outdated material to assess current circumstances or rehabilitation, the satisfaction may be irrational unless there is a rational basis for those current findings.

The Minister is, of course, empowered to make a decision under s 501BA(2) without taking any steps to provide the visa holder with an opportunity to be heard. However, if a significant time has elapsed since the decision proposed to be set aside, a decision not to invite any representations or further evidentiary material from the visa holder may have consequences for the findings that the Minister can properly make in considering whether the power should be exercised.

San Bao Pty Ltd sought constitutional writs of certiorari and mandamus in the High Court after a delegate refused its nomination of Ms Haiming Du for a Subclass 482 (Skills in Demand) visa, the Company having missed the 28-day ART review period. 11 Mar 2026Supreme Court of New South Wales[2026] NSWSC 178Migration: court challenge
Cherrie Civil Engineering (head contractor) sought judicial review of an adjudicator’s determination under the Building and Construction Industry Security of Payment Act 1999 (NSW), alleging the adjudicator failed to consider 600 pages of material filed in a “Quality Documentation” ZIP folder relevant to Variation No 20 descoping valuation. Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v XMBQ [2026] FCAFC 19 (9 March 2026)

9 Mar 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 19Migration: court challenge
The Full Court allowed the Minister’s appeal against orders setting aside a visa cancellation made under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The respondent’s visa had been revoked by the Tribunal under s 501CA, but the Minister later personally cancelled it almost 38 months after that Tribunal decision. The Court held that s 501BA(2) is not subject to an implied reasonable-time limitation, and dismissed the apprehended-bias notice of contention.
Key holding

Section 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) is not subject to an implied temporal limitation that extinguishes the Minister’s power if it is not exercised within a reasonable time after the original s 501CA decision; delay goes to lawful exercise, not jurisdiction.

The central question in this appeal is whether s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) confers a power that is silently extinguished if not exercised within a "reasonable time" after the occurrence of the event which enlivens the power. The answer is that it does not.

The Full Court upheld that approach and the appeal was dismissed with no costs.
Key holding

For Tribunal review jurisdiction, a decision in fact to give a notice is reviewable as a s 88 removal notice if its objective features amount to such a notice, regardless of the decision-maker’s subjective intention or the notice’s legal effectiveness.

All that is required is that a decision to give a notice of some kind was made, and that, having regard to its objective features, the notice that was given amounts, as a matter of fact, to a removal notice as described in s 88(1).

Miglani v Crisp [2026] VSC 47 (18 February 2026)

18 Feb 2026Supreme Court of Victoria[2026] VSC 47Migration: court challenge
Sunny Miglani, a self-represented litigant in immigration detention, appealed under s 148 of the VCAT Act from VCAT’s confirmation that his application to review the VLSC’s closure of his complaint against barrister Ian Crisp was rejected for lack of jurisdiction. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal summarily under s 63 of the Civil Procedure Act 2010 (Vic) because it had no real prospect of success, and refused Mr Crisp’s application for an extended litigation restraint order under s 17 of the Vexatious Proceedings Act 2014 (Vic).
Key holding

VCAT has no jurisdiction to review a decision of the Victorian Legal Services Commissioner to close a complaint under s 277(1) of the LPUL because the LPUL gives a complainant no statutory right of review or appeal to VCAT.

Part 5.6 does not provide any statutory right of review or appeal of a decision to close a complaint to VCAT by a complainant.

DPP v Alama [2026] VCC 132 (16 February 2026)

16 Feb 2026County Court of Victoria[2026] VCC 132Migration: court challenge
Fonotaga Alama pleaded guilty to aggravated burglary and common assault after entering a McDonald’s service area and assaulting a 20-year-old shift manager. The County Court sentenced him to 10 months’ imprisonment combined with an 18-month Community Corrections Order. The court assessed the aggravated burglary as lower than mid-range but the assault as more serious, with significant moral culpability.
Key holding

A custodial sentence combined with a Community Corrections Order may be required for serious aggravated burglary and assault, because a Community Corrections Order alone cannot satisfy the relevant sentencing purposes.

I conclude that a sentence of imprisonment is required in combination with a Community Corrections Order. A Community Corrections Order alone cannot achieve the relevant purposes of sentencing.

Yanunijarra Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC v State of Western Australia [2026] FCAFC 7 (12 February 2026)

12 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 7Migration: court challenge
The Full Court considered whether the State’s inclusion of an expedited procedure statement in notices under s 29 of the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) is a reviewable decision under the ADJR Act or otherwise amenable to judicial review. The primary judge had summarily dismissed the native title parties’ challenge, following Holt v Manzie. The Full Court granted leave to appeal but dismissed the appeal.
Key holding

The inclusion of an expedited procedure statement in a s 29 NTA notice is not a reviewable decision under the ADJR Act or otherwise amenable to judicial review because the statutory provisions operate on the fact the notice includes the statement, not on any anterior Government party decision or opinion.

His Honour concluded that the inclusion of an expedited procedure statement in a notice given under s 29 is not reviewable under the ADJR Act or otherwise amenable to judicial review.

Luong v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCAFC 6 (11 February 2026)

11 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 6Migration: court challenge
The appellant, a Vietnamese citizen, had his visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after a serious violent offence. The AAT later revoked that cancellation, but the Minister personally set aside the AAT decision and cancelled the visa under s 501BA on national-interest grounds. The Full Court dismissed the appellant’s appeal from the primary judge’s refusal of judicial review.
Key holding

The national interest under s 501BA is broad and unconfined, and the Act imposes no mandatory factors on the Minister’s national-interest determination.

The Act does not stipulate any factors to which the Minister must have regard in determining what is in the national interest for the purposes of s 501BA of the Act. What is in the national interest does not readily lend itself to the compartmentalisation of the considerations involved, and it would be contrary to principle for the words "in the national interest" to be given a confined meaning.

Zhu v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, Migrant Services and Multicultural Affairs (No 2) [2026] FCAFC 4 (10 February 2026)

10 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 4Migration: court challenge
In this Full Court costs judgment following dismissal of Mr Zhu’s migration appeal, the Court determined who should pay the costs of the primary proceeding. Mr Zhu sought no costs order on public interest grounds, or alternatively costs fixed under the migration scale in Sch 2; the Ministers sought costs as agreed or taxed. The Court ordered Mr Zhu to pay the first and third respondents’ costs of proceeding BRG193/2022 as agreed or taxed.
Key holding

In a migration proceeding where a party applies for costs under r 22.02, the Court has a discretion to choose a method under r 22.02(2) instead of Sch 2 scale costs if that method is more appropriate.

In a migration proceeding, if an application is made under r 22.02, then the Court must exercise its discretion to determine whether one of the other options in r 22.02(2) is more appropriate than the application of the Schedule 2 scale costs pursuant to r 29.13(1); see r 29.13(3).

ATTORNEY-GENERAL v MCDONALD [2026] SASC 19 (2 February 2026)

2 Feb 2026Supreme Court of South Australia[2026] SASC 19Migration: court challenge
Mr McDonald, already subject to vexatious litigant orders made by Bampton J, sought permission under s 39(1) of the Supreme Court Act 1935 (SA) to sue the Minister for Education for breach of contract and negligence arising from his teaching employment between 1996 and 2003. Gray J refused leave, holding the proposed claim re-litigated the same subject matter already covered by the vexatious litigant orders and that the prior judgments were not void ab initio. The application was dismissed.
Key holding

A vexatious litigant should not be granted leave to institute proceedings that merely re-litigate issues already considered by the Court.

Mr McDonald seeks to re‑litigate issues which have been previously considered by this Court, and he should not be permitted to do so.

January 2026 (65)

Hubzin v The Commissioner for Social Housing; Van Loo v The Commissioner for Social Housing; Irwin v The Commissioner for Social Housing [2026] ACTSC 11 (30 January 2026)

30 Jan 2026Supreme Court of the Australian Capital Territory[2026] ACTSC 11Migration: court challenge
Three long-term ACT public housing tenants challenged decisions under the Growing and Renewing Public Housing Program requiring them to transfer from their homes. The Commissioner conceded the initial decisions denied procedural fairness and consented to them being set aside, and the Court also considered human rights claims under the Human Rights Act 2004 (ACT). The Court extended time, granted declaratory relief, and set aside the initial decisions.
Key holding

A decision made under statutory power without the required procedural fairness is invalid and liable to be set aside.

Where affording procedural fairness is a condition of the grant of a statutory power, and governs the exercise of the power, a failure to comply with the rules will render any decision made, in purported exercise of the power, invalid:

5 Mar 2024Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2024] FedCFamC2G 204Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
This was an application for judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming the refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) (Subclass 500) visa because the applicant did not meet the genuine temporary entrant criterion. The applicant argued the Tribunal's decision was legally unreasonable, particularly the finding that she had stronger ties to Australia than her home country after residing in Australia for 13 years, but the Court found the Tribunal's reasoning was open to it on the evidence and that no jurisdictional error was made out.

FUZ17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs

4 Mar 2024Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2024] FedCFamC2G 191Migration: court challengeMigration
The applicant sought review of a protection visa refusal. The Immigration Assessment Authority (IAA) affirmed the refusal, finding the applicant's claims not credible. The applicant sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision cancelling his subclass 050 Bridging (General) Visa. The applicant, an Iranian-born refugee, sought a writ of habeas corpus after spending 2.5 years in immigration detention without being removed to Iran. The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that this error was not jurisdictional.

The High Court held that although the delegate's decision contained an error of law, the Tribunal conducted a fresh review and made no reviewable error, and the Tribunal had no power to reconsider its own decisions. The appeal was allowed and the application for review dismissed.

Re Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs; Ex parte Durairajasingham

21 Jan 2000High Court of Australia[2000] HCA 1Migration: court challengeMigration
The prosecutor sought prerogative relief in the High Court against a Refugee Review Tribunal decision refusing him a protection visa, arguing the Tribunal failed to take into account relevant considerations and evidence and that s 430(1) of the Migration Act required it to refer to contrary evidence. McHugh J held that s 430(1) does not go to the Tribunal's jurisdiction and that the Tribunal was entitled to reject the claims and evidence. The application for orders nisi was dismissed with costs.

13 Jun 1997High Court of Australia[1997] HCA 22Migration: court challengeMigration
The High Court allowed the Minister's appeals, holding that the Full Court of the Federal Court erred in finding that the Refugee Review Tribunal had misapplied the 'real chance' test for a well-founded fear of persecution. October 1994 (1)

Cunliffe v Commonwealth ("Migration Agents case")

12 Oct 1994High Court of Australia[1994] HCA 44Migration: court challengeMigration
The High Court considered a challenge to Part 2A of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), which requires persons giving immigration assistance to be registered. The plaintiffs argued that the Part was beyond the Commonwealth's legislative power and infringed the implied freedom of political communication and s 92 of the Constitution. The Court held that Part 2A is wholly valid under the aliens power, does not infringe the implied freedom, and any burden on interstate intercourse is proportionate to a legitimate aim.

8 Dec 1992High Court of Australia[1992] HCA 64Migration: court challengeMigration
The plaintiffs, Cambodian nationals who arrived in Australia by boat, challenged the validity of provisions in the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) that mandated their detention pending removal or grant of an entry permit, and that limited the courts' power to order their release. The High Court held that the detention provisions (ss 54L and 54N) were valid as they were non-punitive and within the aliens power, but that s 54R was invalid because it usurped judicial power by preventing courts from ordering the release of unlawfully detained persons.
